newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Polling hours at issue as Albania prepares poll.
newsitem.headline: Polling hours at issue as Albania prepares poll.

text.p: Opposition parties and outside election monitors are hoping that polls can close early in the Albanian general election set for June 29, to minimise the risks of late voting and an after-dark count in the country's lawless state.
Current election law requires the polls to stay open till 9 p.m. -- nearly nightfall.

But pressure for a change is expected when the Organisation for European Security and Cooperation meets in Vienna on Wednesday to discuss its role in aiding and observing the vote it hopes will help to restore order in the former communist state.
Opposition parties boycotted Albania's 1996 vote at the last minute, complaining of fraud, and refused to recognise the result, which OSCE monitors called seriously flawed.

President Sali Berisha's party won by a landslide, but he had to promise a new vote and give the opposition a place in an all-party government early this year after thousands of people, unfamiliar with the new capitalist economy, were duped by investment frauds and public outrage led to a collapse of law and order.
Opposition parties now argue that keeping the polls open late could make it harder to prevent or detect intimidation of late voters or manipulation of the result.

Some members of the central election commission agree and OSCE spokeswoman Melissa Fleming told Reuters: "This (an earlier close) is something we all believe would be key to a successful monitoring operation,"
But Fleming denied Albanian press reports that the OSCE would threaten to withdraw the 450 observers it plans to have watching the vote if polls are not closed earlier.
Violence and tension are mounting as rival political groups attempt to campaign in some territories that can be hostile, under vigilante, rather than police law.
Recent casualties include three policemen and a passer-by burned to death on Tuesday in an attack on police vehicles by heavy weapons on a road in Berat in the south.

Taulant Dedja, Socialist Party representative in Albania's multi-party central election commission, said that with the country in a state of emergency and parliament not sitting, the law on polling times can be changed by presidential decree.
But Genc Pollo, secretary-general of Berisha's Democratic Party, said even this was not possible: a decree would be unconstitutional as parliament has approved the electoral law twice.
